Metro Bus Service in Bangalore 
*141. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the Minister of ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government of Karnataka have submitted a proposal for 
approval to introduce Metro Bus Service in Bangalore; and 
(b) if so, what action Government have taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS MAJOR GENERAL (RETD.) (B. C. 
KHANDURI): (a) and (b) This Ministry had received a proposal from 
Government of Karnataka seeking financial and technical assistance from 
Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (SIDA) for a pilot 
project relating to introduction of Metro Bus System in Bangalore city. The 
proposal was recommended and sent to the Department of Economic Affairs 
(DEA). 

RAJYA  SABHA [28 November, 2002] 
SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Madam, I would like to know from the 
hon. Minister about the recommendation of the Ministry of Surface Transport 
because the Swiss Government has asked for exemption from customs duty; it 
is a 7-million-dollar project. So, I would like to know what their 
recommendation is. I would also like to know, when the recommendation was 
sent. 
MAJOR GENERAL (RETD.) B. C. KHANDURI: Madam, firstly, I wish to 
clarify that in cases like this, my Minist ry gives only the technical aspects of 
the recommendations and further processing is done between the donor agency 
concerned, the DEA and the concerned State Government. This proposal came 
to us on 29th May, 1997 from the State of Karnataka. On 27th June, we 
recommended their proposal, as it was proposed to us, in toto and sent it to the 
Department of Economic Affairs (DEA). Thereafter, it was examined by the 
DEA, in consultation with th State Government. Various correspondences went on 
and till August, 199 as far as our Ministry is concerned, we did not require to 
give any mor inputs. The DEA asked SIDA in August, 1998 to consider the 
proposa SIDA appointed a consultant of Sweden to go into this matter, who, ir 
turn, suggested that the whole thing should be done in four phases. They wanted 
this project to be done in a phased manner. The first phase which would be taken 
up as a pilot project would cost around Rs. 39.4 crores. Thereafter, the 
Government of Karnataka approached this Ministry in October 2002 for 
funding this entire project, through SIDA. We sent the proposal again to the DEA 
with our recommendation that this entire proposal should be funded by SIDA. This 
was done on 24th October, 2000.Thereafter the DEA got in touch with SIDA and the 
correspondences went on between them. And it was only in the month of 
September, 2001—the proposal having started in 1997—that the DEA wrote to 
our Ministry and this had been okayed by SIDA with various observations. In a 
nutshell, SIDA had said that the first pilot project should be undertaken by the 
State Government, with funding through concessional credit and thereafter, 
depending upon the outcome, the phases II, III and IV would be considered. The 
State Government said, "We don't want to do this with our funds. We want the 
pilot projects also to be undertaken by SIDA as a grant", which was not 
agreeable to SIDA. Thereafter SIDA gave an alternative proposal for funding 
through a credit line or a mix of grant and getting loan from some banks. But 
the Government of Karnataka did not agree to that and 
2 

[28 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
said eventually in August 2002 that they would like to do it with their own 
funding. Now, they have made a mini project costing about Rs. 86 lakhs with 
the State Government's funding.This is the position, as far as our information 
goes. 
SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Madam, my second supplementary is this. 
The Swiss Government has agreed to finance the pilot project and they have 
only requested that it should be exem pt from customs duty because the cost 
would be higher. Now, is is a fact that the Swiss Government has agreed to 
fund to fund this project? 
MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B. C. KHANDURI: As per my information and my 
Ministry, the proposal was not accepted by the Karnataka Government and they 
gave two reasons for it. One was the customs duty exemption for the buses 
which was required, was not accepted by the Ministry of Finance. And the 
second thing was that under this proposal there was a dedicated channel for the 
bus routes. The Karnataka Government felt that there was a congestion at various 
places, a separate dedicated route for the buses was not possible. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Shri M. V. Rajasekharan. 
SHRI M. V. RAJASEKHARAN: Madam, Deputy Chairperson, the 
manner in which the whole project is proceeding at a slow pace I do not think it 
would be completed. Would the Government of India consider putting all 
transport systems, wherever it has to be improved, both in the metro cities and 
otherwise, on a fast track? The second thing is, now, I am really surprised to 
hear the hon.' Minister when he said that the Ministry of Finance has not agreed to 
waive the customs duty on this. Now, is it not the responsibility of the Central 
Government to see such projects are given all consideration and support? If they 
consider it as the most important thing to ease the congestion in all the 
metropolitan cities, why should they not take up this project as one of the 
important projects? Would the Ministry consider this proposal? 
MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B. C. KHANDURI: Madam, Deputy Chairperson, two 
issues have been raised. One is that this is going on at a very slow pace and it 
should be put on a faster track. I agree in principle that things should move 
faster and that is why I have given the date and I have also told you about 
various milestones which have occurred during 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [28 November, 2002] 
this processing. Therefore, in principle, we agree that things should move faster, 
but we all know how our system works. Various as puts have to be seen various 
analysis and examination of issues have  to be done. Therefore only certain 
projects are put on a fast track. But to pu t every project on a fast track, I do not 
think it will be possible even if it is desirable. The sec ond thing that the hon. 
Member has said Sir, that the Central Government should also look at the 
transport sector and accept proposal like this. Again, in priciple, I would agree 
with him. But the Central Government has gone much out of its way to fund the 
project in the road sector. A project of Rs. 54,000 crores is now taken up by the 
Centre, totally changing the face of the road system in the country. We have also 
been providing Rs. 1,000 crores per year to the State Governments under the 
Central Road Fund for the State roads. We have also taken up the Pradhan 
Mantri Gramin Sadak Yojna which again is around Rs. 50,000 crores. 
Therefore, a massive amount of investment is going on in the road sector. But, if 
you say that every project that comes up must be accepted, I think, this will not 
be possible.

Statement 
(a) to (c) The Second National Commission on Labour has made its 
recommendations on various aspects of labour viz., review of laws, social 
security, women & child labour, skill de velopment, unorganized sector and 
other matters keeping in view the n eed to enhance economic effciency, 
productivity and competitiveness of industry with due regard to safeguarding 
the interest of working population. The recommendations are based on in-
depth examination and analysis of all the issues. The Government feels that 
the report of the Commission is not contradictory.

Delay in pension reforms 
*146. DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government intend to delay the Reformed 
Pension Plan; 
(b) whether Government would announce the plan before the next 
Budget; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA 
RAJE): (a) to (c) Government do not intend to delay any reforms in the ongoing 
pension schemes.The Government had set up a High-Level Expert Group on 
Pensions.The Group, in its repor t submitted in February 2002, has 
recommended substantive modifications in the existing pension system for 
new entrants.The recommendations made by the Expert Group are being examined 
in their entirety through inter-Ministerial consultations. 
DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: Madam, Chairperson, hon. Minister in her 
reply has stated that the Report of High Level Expert Group on Pension is being 
examined through inter-Ministerial consultations. My question is: What are the 
basic changes that have been recommended by the Expert Group? 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [28 November, 2002] 
SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE: For that, I just like to go first to 
the present Pension Scheme. The present Pension Scheme is a defined benefit 
scheme for which employees actually make no contribution and the pensioner's 
liability is met from the Consolidated Fund of India. The present package of the 
retirement benefits, at the moment, is that, pension is computed at 50 per cent of 
average emoluments of the last 10 months of service. The minimum period of 
service for eligibility to pension is 20 years except for those retiring on 
superannuating pension after 10 years. Then, there is the commutation of pension. 
The Government servant can commute up to 40 per cent of his pension on 
retirement from1.1.1996. This commuted portion of the pension is restored 
after 15 years of the date of the payment of the commuted value. Then, there is 
the death-cum-retirement gratuity, which is payable at 16 1/2 times the 
emoluments, depending on the qualifying service subject to a maximum of Rs. 
3.5 lakhs. Now, emoluments, for this purpose, include basic pay as well as the 
dearness allowance. Now, there was a need for the transition because of the kind 
of expenses that are being incurred. At this moment, before even the Fifth Pay 
Commission happened, the liability, the outflow on pension has increased 
hugely. It has gone up from Rs. 3,272 crores in 1991 to Rs. 8,253 crores in 
1996-97 and finally, to Rs. 22,410 crores in 2001 -02. After the report of the Pay 
Commission, the liabilities have naturally increased. Then, of course, there are a 
number of pensioners and their number is also increasing. This will also make 
that amount increase. The percentage in crease, in the pension expenditure to 
revenue expenditure has gone up from 4.5 per cent in 1991 to 7.25 per cent now in 
2001 -02. So, because of this, it Was felt necessary to introduce some kind of 
reforms and under the proposed scheme we have a contributory-defined benefit 
scheme. Here the scheme comprises basically of two tiers. One is mandatory 
one, where there will be matching contributions from both, that is, the employees 
as well as the employer. Then, there is an optional second tier that will be used 
to promote savings, and for, the second tier, a maximum matching contribution 
of 5 per cent is proposed from the Government. The average emoluments for 
pension are determined with reference to the emoluments drawn by a 
Government servant during the last 36 months of his service. So far, it was not 
there, it was the last ten months' emoluments. Now, the proposal is for 36 
months. Then, the emoluments are to include the dearness allowance. 
This is going to be clubbed. (Interruptions) No, no. He wanted to know 
the difference. So, I am giving him the difference, what difference is

there. In addition to the basic pay, the emoluments include dearness 
allowance. The increase in inflation will be kept at 5 per cent. No wage 
indexation has been recommended here and no addition to qualifying service 
has been recommended, because, in the earlier scheme, you could add five 
years to it. But, in this scheme, there is no addition, and pension will be 
payable only from the date of the superannuation.There is a second exit point, 
which has been provided here and that second exit point is after attaining the age 
of 50 years. The employee can either take the accrued pension then at 60 years or 
he can take an immediate pension which will be reduced according to our table.

*145. DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO: W ill the Minister of ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to bring forward a new legislation or 
amend the existing laws to provide for deterrent punishment for drunken driving 
which is the major cause of accidents; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS MAJOR GENERAL (RETD.) (B.C. 
KHANDURI): (a) and (b) Provisions exist in the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 to 
deter and punish the act of drunken driving. Under Section 185 of the Motor 
Vehicles Act, while driving or attempting to drive a motor vehicle, if a person 
has, in his blood, alcohol exceeding 30 mg. per 100 ml of blood detected in a test 
by a breath analyzer, he shall be punishable: 
(i) for the first offence with imprisonment for a term which may extend 
to six months, or with fine which may extend to two thousand 
rupees, or with both; and 
(ii) for a second or subsequent offence, if committed within three years 
of the commission of the previous similar offence, with 
imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine 
which may extend to three thousand rupees, or with both. 
Certain amendments making the above provision more stringent are 
contemplated.

*152.  DR.T.SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to State: 
(a) whether the Standing Committee on Food, Civil Supplies and Public 
Distribution has directed Government to increase the export of sugar as more 
than 115 lakh tonnes of sugar was lying in various godowns and warehouses in 
the country; 
(b) whether availability of sugar during the last financial year was more 
than 270 lakh tonnes, out of which the internal consumption was only to the 
tune of about 160 lakh tonnes; 
(c) if so, what were the reasons for not exporting the extra sugar; and 
(d) the steps being taken to implement the suggestions? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) Yes, Sir, The Committee has 
recommended that the Government should encourage export of sugar even by 
amending the Sugar Development Fund Act, 1982 and thereby giving relief to 
sugar mill owners. 
(b) The sugar season is reckoned from October to September. During the 
sugar season 2000-2001, with the carry over stock of 93.40 lakh tonnes and 
the sugar production of 185.10 lakh tonnes, the total availability of sugar in the 
country was 278.50 lakh tonnes, as against the internal consumption of 162.00 
lakh tonnes. In additions, about 9.87 lakh tonnes of sugar was exported.Thus at 
the end of the season i.e. 30th September, 2001, the closing stock of sugar was 
around 106.63 lakh tonnes, 
(c) and (d) The export of sugar is undertaken under Open General Licence 
(OGL) by various private parties and Public Sector Undertakings etc. As 
reported by DGCI&S, Kolkata, during the sugar season 2001-2002 (upto July 
2002), a quantity of about 8.91 lakh tonnes has already been exported. However, 
as per information received from the trade circles, the total export of sugar during 
the sugar season 2001-2002 was 9.77 lakh tonnes (provisional). 
35 

RAJYA  SABHA [28 November, 2002] 
In order to boost the export of sugar, the Government has taken the 
following measures: 
(i) Sugar meant for export has been exempted from the levy 
obligation. 
(ii) The quantity of sugar released for export is treated as advance free-
sale release to be adjusted in the free-sale stocks of the sugar 
factories after a period of 18 months. 
(iii) Duty Entitlement Pass Book (DEPB) at the rate of 4% of the FOB 
value of export of sugar has been allowed. 
(iv) Hitherto only mill white sugar was being exported. It has been 
clarified that in addition to mill white sugar the sugar mills/ 
exporters can also export raw sugar under the present Export Import 
(EXIM) policy. 
(v) The Government has amended the Sugar Development Fund Act, 
1982 so as to provide for defraying the expenditure from the Sugar 
Development Fund on internal transport & freight charges to the 
sugar factories on the export shipment of sugar. This amendment has 
come into force with effect from 21.6.2002 and necessary rules have 
also been notified.

Leakage of radioactive substances 
t893. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether government are aware of the fact that several incidents of 
leakage of the most sensitive radioactive substances of atomic plants have taken 
place in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that the cons truction and maintenance of atomic 
plants is so poor that the incidents like Chernobil are feared any time; 
(d) if so, whether Government have formulated any scheme to improve 
maintenance and safety of the plants; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENTS OF ATOMIC 
ENERGY AND SPACE (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) and (b) 
Yes, Sir. There were a few incidents of leakage of tritiated heavy water from the 
nuclear power plants in India. None of these had any significant impact on 
public and environment. Details are available in the Annual Report of Atomic 
Energy Regulatory Board and are as follows: 
(1) Subsequent to a leak in a moderator heat exchanger of Unit-2 of the 
Rajasthan Atomic Power Station on May 05, 1998, heavy water containing 
tritium got released into the Rana Pratap Sagar  
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
52 

[28 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
Lake. The annual radiation dose to the public due to the release was 25 
microsievert compared to the annual  dose limit of 1000 microsievert 
prescribed by Atomic Energy Regulator y Board. Though release was above 
the limit prescribed by AERB, the impact of the release was negligible. 
(2) On March 26,1999 heavy water leaked from Unit-2 of Madras Atomic 
Power Station due to failure of a seal plug during coolant channel inspection. 
The incident lead to release of some radioactive through the stack, which was 
well within the limit prescribed by AERB. 
(3) On April 15, 2000 tritium containing heavy water leaked from the 
moderator system of Unit-2 of Narora Atomic Power Station into the reactor 
building. This leak occurred due to the failure of the gasket of flang joint. 
The activity released was within the prescribed limit. 
(4) On June 16, 2000 a tube leak occurred in one of the heat exchangers of 
steam generator No. 1 of Unit-1 of Madras Atomic Power Station resulting in 
release of some amount of tritium into the environment through liquid route. 
The activity released was within the limit prescribed by AERB. 
(5) On September 26, 2000 there was one incident of release of tritium 
activity from Rajasthan Atomic Power Station to Rana Pratap Sagar Lake. 
The activity released was well within the limits prescribed by AERB. 
(6) On November 20,2001 the end fitting blank of one of the coolant 
channels of Narora Atomic Power Station Unit-1 leaked tritium containing 
heavy water.The incident did not result in any release of activity in excess of 
the prescribed limit. 
(c) to (e) No, Sir. The nuclear power plants in India are designed, constructed 
and operated as per the provisions of prescribed safety codes and standards. 
The maintenance practices and operati ng procedures are as per approved 
norms and are scrupulously followed. In view of these reas ons, an accident 
like that which occurred at Chernobyl is highly unlikely.

Statement 
Norms for opening post offices 1. Norms for opening 
Extra Departmental Branch Post Offices: 1.1 Population: (a) In Normal 
Areas: 
3000 population in a group of villages (including the PPO village)

500 population in an individual village or 1000 population in a 
group of villages.

(a) In Normal Areas:

3 Kms.

Areas, the minimum distance limit can be relaxed by the 
Directorate in cases where such re laxation is warranted by special 
circumstances which should be clearly explained while submitting a 
proposal.

(a) In Normal Areas: 
The minimum anticipated revenue will be 33 1/3% of the cost. 
(b) In Hilly,Tribal, Desert and Inaccessible Areas: 
The minimum anticipated income will be 15% of the cost. 2. Criteria 
for upgrading/opening Departmental Sub Post Offices: 
(a) In Rural Areas: 
The minimum work load of the Extra Departmental Branch Post 
Office, proposed to be upgraded, should be five hours per day. The 
permissible limit of annual loss is Rs. 2400/- in Normal rural areas and 
Rs. 4800/- in Tribal and Hilly areas. 
(b) In Urban Areas: 
In Urban areas, the post office should initially be self-supporting, and, at 
the time of the first annual review, it should show a 5% profit to be 
eligible for further retention. 
The minimum distance between two post offices should be 1.5 
Kms. in cities with a population of 20 lakhs and above, and 2 Kms. in 
other Urban Areas. No two delivery offices, however, should be 
closer than 5 Kms. for each other.

Call Tariff of Fixed Telephones 
904. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJ ARY: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that while in the case of mobile phones, the call 
tariff are inversely proportiona l to the number ofecalls, i.e. more the calls, 
lesser the tariff which is an internationally accepted commercial prudence; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that as against the above norms, the call tariff of 
fixed telephone lines increases direclty in proportion to the number of calls, i.e. 
more the calls, higher the tariff; 
(c) whether Government are considering to reverse tariff in respect of the 
fixed telephones in the manner adopted for mobile phone; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY 
(SHRIMATI SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) Airtime charges in case of mobile 
subscribers in only one component of mobile tariff. The service providers are 
offering various alternative tariff options where the monthly rental and per 
minute airtime charges may be different depending upon the usage pattern of 
the subscribers. While in most tariff schemes, call charges per minute remain 
constant irrespective of the number of calls, some Service Providers are also 
offering tariff schemes where the per minute call charges are inversely proportional 
to the number of calls. However, it is difficult to establish an exact relationship 
between airtime charges and the actual usage due to large number of tariff plans 
being offered by different operators. 
(b) The call tariff for fixed telephone lines is based on slab-system, under 
which call rates beyond 500 calls are uniform.The charges are less in case of low 
user subscribers in whose case the affordability criteria have been taken into 
consideration.

TRAI Act, 1997 as amended by TRAI (Amendment) Act, 2000, and

Indian Labour Conference 
971. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Indian Labour Conference was held at New Delhi in the 
month of September, 2002; 
(b) if so, the details of the delegates participated in the conference and 
the points discussed therein; 
(c) the outcome of the discussions held in the conference; 
(d) whether Government have taken any further action on the points 
discussed in the conference; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR 
(SHRI ASHOK PRADHAN): (a) Yes, Sir. The 38th Session of the Indian 
Labour Conference was held at New Delhi on 28-29 September, 2002. 
(b) The Conference was attended by delegates from Central Trade 
Union Organisations (Bhartiya Mazdoor Sangh, Indian National Trade Union 
Congress, Centre of Indian Trade Unions, Hind Mazdoor Sabha, All India 
Trade Union Congress, United Trade Union Centre-LS, United Trade Union 
Congress and National Front of Indian Trade Unions), Central Employers' 
Organisations (Council of Indian Employers, Confederation of Indian 
Industries, All India Manufacturers' Organisation, Laghu Udyog Bharati, 
Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Associated 
Chamber of Commerce and Industry of India), concerned Central Ministries/ 
Deptts. and State Governments/Union Territories. The Conference discussed 
the following issues: 
(i)  Impact of globalization on the Indian economy particularly on 
employment, and how to meet the challenges. 
(ii) Social Safety Net. 
(iii) Disinvestment Policy of the Government. 
128 

[28 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(iv) Problems and challenges being faced by the small-scale industries 
and their remedies. 
(v) Report of Second National Commission on Labour. 
(c) The following main views emerged out of the discussions held in the 
conference:— 
(i) there is need for an in-depth review of the impact of globalisation 
on the Indian economy and for social dialogue on strategies to be 
adopted for facing the challenges of globalisation. 
(ii) there is need for a comprehe nsive legislation for and increased 
spending on social security. 
(iii) there is a need for an overall review of the Disinvestment Policy 
keeping national interest in mind. 
(iv) there is need for simplificati on and rationalisation of labour laws 
applicable to tiny and small scale industry and provision of social 
security measures like insurance,  medical coverage and disability 
benefits. 
(v) there is need for introduction of an umbrella legislation for workers 
in the unorganised sector. 
(vi) there is need for creation of a Skill Development Fund for training/ 
re-training of workers. 
(vii) Despite divergence of opinions on the recommendations of the 
National Commission on Labour, there was unanimity of views on 
certain recommendations viz., umbrella legislation for workers in 
unorganised sector, creation of skill development fund for training 
& retraining, encouragement of sm all scale industry, agri-business 
and rural sector for higher employment generation, consolidation 
of social security legislations an d establishment of social security 
system etc. 
(d) to (e) While formulating policies/programmes on matter* relating to 
labour, the recommendations of the conference are given due consideration 
by the Government.

995. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that despite endorsing Government's stand on 
liberalization of labour laws, the Second National Commission on Labour has put 
conditions on easier retrenchement, closure of establishments, the hire and fire 
policy and engaging of contract labour; and

workers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR 
(SHRI ASHOK PRADHAN): (a) and (d)The Second National Commission on 
Labour has recommended that prior permission is necessary in respect of lay-off 
and retrenchment in an establishment of any employment size. However, in the 
case of establishments employing 300 or more workers if the lay off is continued 
for more than 30 days, post facto permission of the appropriate Government 
shall be required. The provisions of Chapter V-B pertaining to permission for 
closure should be made applicable to all establishments if they are employing 
300 or more workers. 
In respect of the contract labour, the Commission has recommended that 
Contract Labour shall not be engaged fo r core production/services activities. 
However, for sporadic seasonal demand, the employer may engage temporary 
labour for core production/serviec activity. 
Recommendations of the Commission are under consideration of the 
Government of India.

1006. SHRI RAMACHANDRAKHUNTIA:Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the aims and objectives for which the National 
Commission on Population was set up; 
(b) what have been its achievements till date; and 
(c) by when the National Population Policy is likely to be finalized and 
announced? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) The aims and objectives of the 
National Commission on Population are to: 
(i) review, monitor and give directions for the implementation of the 
National Population Policy with a view to meeting the goals set out in 
the policy. 
(ii) promote synergy between demographic, educational, environmental 
and developmental programmes so as to hasten population 
stabilization. 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [28 November, 2002] 
(iii) promote inter-sectoral coordination in planning and implementation 
across government agencies of the Central and State Governments, to 
involve the civil society and the private sector and to explore the 
possibilities of international cooperation in support of the goals set out 
in the Policy. 
(iv) facilitate the development of a vigorous people's movement in 
support of this national effort. 
(b)The main achievements of the National Commission on Population are 
given below: 
(i) On the basis of the decisions ta ken at the first Conference of the 
Commission and the Strategic Support Group of Secretaries of the 
concerned Departments, eight Working/Advisory Groups were 
constituted by the NCR The report/recommendations of these 
Groups have been forwarded to the concerned Departments and 
taken into consideration, to the extent possible, in the sectoral 
programmes for the Tenth Five Year Plan. 
(ii) A thorough review of the implementation of the national Family 
Welfare programme in the high fertility States and at the national level. 
(iii) Identification of 133 districts having TFR>3.5 for focused action for 
population stabilization followed by a conference of DMs of these 
districts to discuss and decide about various matters relating to 
population stabilization. 
(iv) Selection of social, economic and demographic indicators for 
monitoring purpose. 
(v) Conference of Demographic Res earch Organisations for integrating

Anantapur district of Andhra Pradesh 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Madam, 
Anantapur District in Andhra Pradesh is one of the backward districts in the

arid and rain-shadow zone. The annual rainfall in this district is very low, and

then, of the treatable area of 12 lakh hectares, only 3.8 lakh hectares have 
been covered under the watershed programme. This is a very low coverage, 
by any standards. The State Government is doing all that it can, and has also, 
recently, announced a special package to take up both short-term and long-
term  measures to mitigate the drought conditions prevailing  in the

Evacuation of people from forest 
SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY (Karnataka): Madam, crores of 
people, mostly belonging to the socially and economically weaker sections of 
the society, have been living in the reserved forest areas in various parts of 
the country for centuries, tilling the soil and in employment, generated 
through the forest produce, and in peace and harmony with Nature. For 
example, a number of families in the 'Malnad' region, spread over a few 
districts of Karnataka, namely, Kodagu, Dakshina Kannada, Uttara Kannada, 
Chickmagalore, Hassan and Shimoga, have been tilling forest land for 
generations. A total of 14,848.83 hectares of land is under cultivation.

an encroachment and a threat to the eco -system. Therefore, on the ground of 
protecting the flora and fauna, they are being uprooted from their hearth. In 
the process, they are deprived of their land and the source of livelihood. The 
order of the hon. Supreme Court of India,  for clearing the forest land of such 
encroachments, has given an impetus to the evacuation exercise. Having been 
deprived of their livelihood, the affected farmers have no option but to 
commit suicide, as in the case of farmer s in a number of States, hit by natural 
calamities. Laws are made for protecting the interests of the people and not to 
jeopardise their safety and livelihood. Since it is a human problem, the 
relevant laws may be suitably amended to protect their interests. 
The Central Government may, th erefore, immediately frame a 
suitable legislation, in consultation with the State Government, to protect 
their interests.

City Challenge Fund for Development of Urban Areas 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Karnataka): Madam, the urban 
development and municipal sector do not have many Centrally-Sponsored 
Schemes. There are basically four schemes at present, viz., IDSMT, SJSRY, 
Mega City and Augmented Water Supply Scheme. The major problems in 
most urban areas today are public health and sanitation. The activities that are 
needed to improve the situation in this regard are: (a) much better solid 
221 

RAJYA SABHA [28 November, 2002] 
waste management practices and (b) much greater coverage of underground 
drainage. 
As regards (a), based on court pronouncement, the Government of 
India has promulgated rules, etc. However, the major recommendations of the 
court and the court a ppointed commission, viz., the creation of Solid Waste 
Management Mission at the Government of India level and a Centrally-
sponsored scheme, have not been acted upon. Similarly, underground 
drainage is in a very poor shape in mo st of the States. In Karnataka, except 
for 20 towns and cities having both internal sewer system and sewage 
treatment plants, the rest, viz., 197 cities/towns have woefully inadequate 
underground drainage coverage. Both these involve capital expenditure far 
beyond the capacity of most of the ULBs and, therefore, the case for a 
Centrally-sponsored scheme for both these activities is a sound one. 
The City Challenge Fund proposed to be introduced by the 
Government of India has a minimum population size of one million. To have 
dispersed urbanisation, what is required is improvement in many small and 
medium towns. The City Challenge Fund, therefore, should look at cities with 
population of five lakhs and above. Thank you.

Mention is pertaining to giving world heritage status to Hyderabad.

the imperative need to secure the status of Heritage City to Hyderabad. Hon.

twelfth Century. This city has evolved from the fortress town Golconda, 
taking birth in 1591. Hyderabad is built around Charminar, a Qutubshahi

are there in Hyderabad. Last week I had been to the UNESCO, discussed with

and function, and having preserved the spatial arrangements and structures.

Implementation of Mid-Day Meals Scheme for School Children 
SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI (Nominated): Madam, my Special 
Mention is relating to implementation of Mid-day Meal Scheme for school 
children, under the National Programme of Nutritional Support for Primary 
Education. 
It is a sad fact that the level of  under-nutrition in India is among the 
highest in the world. About fifty per ce nt of the of all children are estimated 
to be under-nourished, and one-third of our babies are born with low birth 
weight. In 1995, the Central Government introduced the National Programme 
of Nutritional Support for Primary Education. Under this programme, 
primary school children were supposed to  receive 3 kgs. of grain per month. 
Cooked mid-day meals were to be intr oduced within two years. Five years 
later, only a few State Governments have introduced cooked mid-day meals. 
On 28 m November, 2001, the Supreme Court had ordered all State 
Governments to introduce cooked mid-day meals in all primary schools, 
within six months. Mid-day meals are very important because they boost 
school attendance. They protect childre n from hunger. They help to break 
caste barriers, prejudices, as children learn to sit together and share a meal. A 
recent study found that af ter the introduction of mid-day meal earlier this 
year, the attendance of girl students ha d increased by 35% in Barmer district 
of Rajasthan. A well-planned mid-day meal programme would cost about Re. 
1 pr child, per day, to the State Government, that is, around Rs. 400 crores per 
year. The future of 20 million children is at stake. The Central Government 
should, therefore, assist the State G overnments to ensure that their own 
programme is actually implemented. Children must become a priority, if the 
nation has to march forward with its head held high.

.SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasthan): Madam, I would like to mention

externally aided projects -- 0.5%; (f) la nd reforms -- 0.5%]; special problems 
7.5%.

following factors as well. These are: 1.  Area: Since the cost of delivery of 
service is more due to larger area and low population density, weightage for 
larger area is justified; 2. Desert: Si milar weightage should be given to a 
desert-State, as is given to hilly-States. For example, Rajasthan has 60% of

population; 5. Per capita income and per capita outlay of plan, compared to 
national average; 6. lower credit-deposit ratio, compared to the national 
coverage; 7. Investment in the State Enterprise of the Central Government, 
situated in the State.

above-mentioned factors whil e transferring grants to States, and also, at the 
same time, amend the Gadgil-Mukherjee Formula, accordingly.

SHORT DURATION DISCUSSION 
On grave situation arising in West Asia threatening world peace and security 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Mr. Vice-Chairman, 
Sir, thank you for giving me this opportunity to raise the Short Duration 
Discussion on the grave situation arising in West Asia threatening world 
peace and security. Sir, there are two se nsitive areas in West Asia where the 
tension is escalated. One is, of course, the problem which is going on between 
Israel and Palestine. And the other area is Iraq where, just now, the inspectors 
appointed by the United Nations, as per the Security Council Resolution No. 
1441, are visiting. And, in that context, we would like to express our views as 
to what role India can play to defuse the tension and also to ensure that it does 
not further escalate and also lead to some sort of armed confrontation. 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, in th e areas of foreign policy and 
international relations, over the years, we have developed a broad consensus, 
and irrespective of the political parties occupying the Treasury Benches, 
hardly there has been any major di fferences in our approach to the 
international problems, in our relations with various countries, in our 
immediate neighbourhood or outside and, especially, in our relationship with 
the Super Powers. In one way, the second  half of the last century is unique, 
because in that second half of the la st century, the world witnessed no world-
wide conflicts, except some regional conflicts, in stark contrast to the first 
half of that century, where two world wars took place. In  the second half, 
especially in the 80s, world has moved closer with the end of the cold 
232 

[28 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
war. Therefore, the perceptions with which we used to function, have 
undergone radical changes over the years. Long before the dismantling of the 
Berlin Wall, who could imagine that a day will come when all those littoral 
States around the Mediterranean, who dominated the world history by 
constantly engaging themselves in fratricidal wars will think in terms of 
common market, common currency, co mmon security policy and common 
external relations. This is the level of the changes which have taken place. 
Collapse of the Berlin Wall came much later, but it has added to that process. 
In this context, when the situation was becoming really grim, especially in the 
last four years when no UN Inspectors could visit Iraq, after the adoption of 
the latest Resolution N0.1441, a team of UN Inspectors, as per the newspaper

give its report. On the basis of that the international community, specially the 
Security Council, will respond appropri ately. But, in the intervening period 
one thing has happened. I would like to draw the attention of the Foreign 
Minister to this . I would also like to have his assessment of the situation. 
Sir, you are aware of the fact th at on humanitarian ground, the UN 
Security Council used to allow Iraq to sell a part of their oil to buy essentials, 
especially food items, medicines and other things. Since the sanction was 
imposed in the early 90s and it was very rigorous, as it was issued under 
Chapter VII of trie Charter of the United Nations, which is mandatory to 
everybody. Therefore, India and ma ny other countries pleaded that on 
humanitarian grounds relief should be given to them. They depand mainly on 
the oil resources and they should be allowed to export a part of that resources 
to earn enough foreign exchange to main tain themselves. Up to now, subject 
to correction by the hon. Minister, if I am wrong, in 13 phases this concession 
has been given at the regular interval of six months. But, I read from the 
newspaper reports that on last Monday this extension and this facility has 
been given for nine days only. It will come to an end on 4 m December. I do 
not know whether it is actually correct or not. Perhaps, it is linked with the 8m 
December, by which date Iraq is expected to comply with the Inspectors. But, 
so far as I understand, the Inspectors' team are expected to give their report 
by February. So, what is the rationality? I understand it was hardly debated in 
the Security Council and the Security Council passed it unanimously, What 
would be the implications and what would be the significance of it? That has 
to be assessed. I would like the hon. Minister of External Affairs to throw 
some light on this

recently. Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I welc ome the Statement of the hon. Prime

would like to have. Nobody, however justified the other country maybe, can 
intervene to decide what type of Go vernment, what type of leadership a

big powers enjoy special powers, we have no differr \ with them. Therefore,

position should be clarified. We have very excellent relationship with the 
United States of America. There is no  doubt that with the changing world 
situation, this relationship has better significance. It is not that we did not 
have good relationship earlier. From day one, United States of America is one 
of the largest trading partners of India. Whether it was controlled regime or 
liberalised regime, the largest num ber of technical and financial 
collaborations we had with any individual country is with the United States of 
America. Even in case of our requirement, starting from the days of PL-480 
when we had inadequacy of food, we r eceived their support, mainly, with the 
backing of one great American citi zenry, about whom there was some 
misunderstanding at some point of time in some part of this country, 
McNamara. During his last phase as the Governor of World Bank, I had the 
privilege of working with him. Through his strong support, we got the 
International Development Assistance, through which Indian agriculture got a 
tremendous momentum as a consequenc e of which we have become self-
sufficient. Not only we have become self-sufficient in our foodgrains

things are there. But, at the same time, it is equally true that this country has 
accepted an independent foreign policy. Whatever we feel correct, ji ', proper, 
we do not hesitate to espress so.    Th erefore, the role, which we can play, of 
course, within the

limitations, which we have, we should try to play. After all, one need not

establishment is the only voice of US A. Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I have a

M America is never wholly herself unless she is engaged in high

conveyed, and as per the newspaper reports, I find that the Iraqi Minister toas

as per the Resolution of the Security Council. But, what disturbs us when we

whether those omissions or lapses would

be used as a reason for launching an aggression as apprehended by Iraq's

most Bush told in his inaugural addr ess, that is: "Goodwill begets goodwill,

Now, coming to the other point, Mr. vice-Chairman Sir, I would not

I understand, the Government of India has very correctly pointed out that we 
stand by the causes of the Palestinians - we have no enmity with Israel, we

I shall conclude by making anot her observation, made by another 
great  American  President,   I  think  he  was  the  second  President,  John

Adams. He was the first occupant of the present White House. He moved into

against Iraq is that it is has weapons of mass destruction, it is a threat to its

SHRI S. VIDUTHALAI VIRUMBI : Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, the 
Short Duration Discussion brought before us is, 'on the grave situation arising 
in West Asia threatening world peace and security'. 
We have to look at the situation from the world peace and security 
angle. Everybody knowsthat India had,  has and will have cordial relations 
with the West Asian countries, partic ularly Iraq, because even in the 
Organisation of the Islamic Countries, Iraq stood by India. The situation, 
now, is that the present discussion is taking place because of the observations 
made on this issue by our hon. Prime Minister. Sir, India's stand is that one 
should not impose one's will on other countries; and Iraq 
250 

[28 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
should comply with the UN Resolution, and destroy the weapons of mass 
destruction. Also, once the UN team is satisfied that Iraq has complied with 
the Resolution, the sanction against Iraq should be lifted. We say that 
because, otherwise, it will affect the p eace and security of the region. On the 
eve of our Independence, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehruji founded the bipolar 
system. Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru from India, Marshal Tito from Yugoslavia 
and Mr. Nasser from Egypt, were the architects of the non-aligned 
movement. When the Cold War is over, when liberalisation is taking place, 
there are bound to be di fferences of opinion among countries, and also, 
within a country. The developed countrie s have, so far, allowed only the free 
flow of capital. The developed countries have not allowed the free flow of 
labour throughout the world. Therefore, there is a difference of opinion. How 
is it going to affect the world? Iraq  owes to Russia 8 billion dollars. Russia 
has got a contract for rehabilitation of the oilfields in Iraq. Some of the 
important oilfields are West Qurna - the richest deposit in the world -, 
Majnoo and Nahr Umar. When it is so, Russia has got an economic interest in 
Iraq. That is also a point. We will have to see to it. Now, the UN team has 
inspected. Today, through the electroni c media, we came to understand that 
the UN Team is satisfied with its inspection. I do not know whether they are 
thoroughly satisfied, because there was a condition that they should not enter 
the mosques and the palace of Saddam Hussain. We also do not know 
whether the UN Team had complied with the conditions put forth by Iraq. 
But, the report is that the UN Team is satisfied with its inspection. But, I 
would like to emphasise on the point that despite the fact that the UN Team is 
satisfied, one is not sure whether the wa r against Iraq will be averted or not. 
It is a question of debate. Why do I say so? I would like to point out that in 
the first week of May, there was information from the US... (Time- bell) I 
will take only three minutes, Sir. ...interruptions)... Sir, I would like to quote 
from The Hindu. The UN Secretary of State, Collin Powell, on Sunday, the 
7m May, 2002, said, "The Bush Administration's policy on leadership change 
in Iraq is separate, distinct, differe nt, from allowing the weapons to be 
inspected in Iraq." That means, the inspection has been delinked from the 
question leadership change in Iraq. That is why we have a doubt in our mind 
whether the war against Iraq would be averted or not, despite the fact that the 
UN Team is satisfied with its inspection. Sir, they further say, "The United 
States reserves its opinion to do, whatever it believes might be appropriate to 
see if there can be a regime change. Th e U.S. policy is like this. Regardless 
of what the Inspectors do, I repeat, regardless of what the Inspectors do, the 
251 

RAJYA SABHA [28 November, 2002] 
people of Iraq; the people of the region would be better off with a different 
regime in Baghdad. This is what was announced by the Secretary of State, 
Mr. Collin Powell. So, even if the U.N. Inspection Team is satisfied, we 
doubt whether war could be averted. Now, what is the role of India in this? In 
this connection, the observations made by the hon. Prime Minister have been 
hailed throughout India, cutting across party-lines. But the point is, this 
observation should be translated into action. This is what we expect from the 
Government. The people of Iraq are suffering a lot. In order to save the 
people of Iraq, in fact, to save the people of all the developing countries, some 
basic facilities should be provided to them. In- developing countries, 
unemployment is on the increase, and even basic facilities are not available 
there. In Iraq, even the life-saving dr ugs are not available, and they are 
suffering day in, day out. We want that India should become a permanent 
member of the Security Council. This is my suggestion. And we will always 
stand by the Government on this. I think the entire House will agree with me 
on this. (Interruptions)... If India becomes a permanent member of the 
Security Council, then, I think these type of things would be averted by veto. 
We should save the people of Iraq by restoring democracy there. We should 
see to it that multi-party system is restored there. It is for the people of Iraq 
and nobody else, to decide how to restore democracy there. 
SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN (Karnataka): Sir, I thank you very much 
for giving me this opportunity. The situation in West Asia is really grave and 
a cause of concern for all the peace -loving countries of the world, 
particularly, India. Whenever the world is  threatened with war, India, as the

tradition in mind. It is very clear from the utterances of the U.S 
Administration that it wants a war. I am afraid, even if the Weapon Inspectors

biological or nuclear weapons, America will, definitely, find some excuse to 
create a situation for war. We have to be careful about this. We have very

India has got an independent foreign policy. India has a role to play in the 
world community. We are the largest de mocracy in the world.   We value 
democracy more than America.   America plays a dual role

[28 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
as far as its foreign policy is concerne d. In certain countries, America wants

in which the Israel is attacking, the way it is occupying the places

SHRI SHANKAR ROY CHOWDHURY (West Bengal) : Mr.-'Vice-
Chairman, Sir, the discussion this evening is on the grave situation in West 
Asia, threatening world peace and security. I think the scope of the discussion 
should be extended to include the situation in Asia and its effects on Indian 
national interest because, I think, when we study or examine the situation in 
West Asia it should primarily be to see what effects it wijfc'have on our 
national interests in that region and elsewhere. 
 
In my view, West Asia contains the following factors which have a 
bearing on our national interests and we should follow this with cold 
calculated policy decisions to the exclusion of all emotionalism on the issue. 
These are : firstly, Oil. Secondly, the safety, security and stability of the large 
Indian expatriate community in the West Asian countries and its 
neighbourhood. Thirdly, the war against terrorism and fourthly, the 
availability of technology from countries  in West Asia. Coming to oil, it is 
very clear that the overall reason be hind America's attempts or America's 
stated design to attack Iraq is to gain possession of its oil resources. Iraq 
possesses one of the largest oil resources in the world. It is not merely 
attacking Iraq that will serve America's purpose, it has to ensure a regime 
change. There is no other alternative if America is to obtain possession of the 
oil resources of Iraq. Should  there be a regime change in Iraq, I think, Iraq 
will split into three entities. In the north, you will have some kind of Khurdish 
Autonomous Reoublic, in the Centre, you will have the Rump of Iraq and in 
the south, you will probably have some kind of Shia Republic aligned with 
Iran. Whatever be the outcome of such a war, it will cause tremendous 
instability with great adve rse effects on the Indian  economy because it will 
disturb our national interests which, centred around, ensure an uninterrupted 
supply of oil for our economy, as well as a great blow to the stability to the 
Indian community in this area which do es make a large remittance of foreign 
exchange, so essential for our economy. As far as the war against terror is 
concerned,  the war,  which India is waging, which

SHRI YASHWANT SINHA : Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I am grateful 
to Shri Pranab Mukherjeeji and all the other 15 Members who have 
participated in this debate. We have had a very rich debate on the issue which 
the House took up for consideration this afternoon and as Shri Rajeev 
Shuklaji has said, I do not think the mood or the consensus within this House 
is in doubt beyond anyone's grasp. I only hasten to add that there is no 
disconnect or discordance between the policies followed by the Government 
and the mood expressed in this House, at least on this particular issue. Pranab 
Babu was quite right in saying - and indeed some other Members also - that 
India's foreign policy has always been based on national consensus. This is 
one issue where we keep aside our im mediate political differences and every 
political party endeavours to look at it from the prism of national interest and 
in the long-term.    And that has been the great 
269 

RAJYA SABHA [28 November, 2002] 
strength of India's foreign policy and I believe, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, that 
this has come about because India's foreign policy has been rooted in the 
freedom struggle which this country waged. 
Our leaders, at that point of time, had evolved a policy which 
independent India was supposed to follow. This policy was deeply 
influenced by the way India conducted its freedom movement, because 
India's freedom movement, Sir, is unique in the annals of world history and, 
therefore, that idealism, which informed  the freedom movement of India, is 
an idealism which has been the hallmark of our foreign policy throughout. 
National interest, as General Roy Chowdhury said, has never been given a 
go-by. At every point of time, this country, its Government of the day, has 
kept national interest clearly in mind. But, as Pandit Nehru once said, the 
idealism of today is the realism of tomorrow, and, therefore, we have to keep 
in mind our long-term interest and keep in mind the idealism which has 
always informed our foreign policy, and also not discard, even for a moment, 
our very important national interests which, ultimately, our foreign policy is 
supposed to subserve. 
Having said that, Sir, I would like to begin by a statement which the 
Prime Minister made in New York, when he had gone there to attend the 
meeting of the UN General Assembly. This was in September when, in the 
UN General Assembly, in the U.S. and, perhaps, in the rest of the world, the 
most important issue which was dominating the debate, the most important 
issue which was on everyone's mind, was the issue of Iraq. When he met the 
Press there, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, he was asked a question on India's 
policy on Iraq, and this is what he said: "One, India has vital and strategic 
interests in the Gulf, and a large India diaspora lives and works in that 
region. India has also had a historical relationship with Iraq". He went on to 
say, "At the same time, we fully understand the international community's 
desire to see the relevant UN Resolutions on weapons of mass destruction 
complied with fully. We believe that sanctions against Iraq should be lifted, 
in tandem with full and effective compliance by Iraq, of the UN Resolution". 
These were the three sutras in which the Prime Minister stated the position of 
India during that Press conference. 
Then, the UN Security Council Resolution was adopted, and, more recently - as Members have quoted, a nd as Prof. R.B.S. Verma, from our side, has quoted, - on November 19, the Prime Minister, on the occasion of 
270 

[28 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Guru Nanak Jayanti, made a Statement, which was widely published in the 
newspapers, and set forth very clearly the point of view of this country. 
Subsequently, the official spokesperson of the Ministry of External Affairs 
replied to a question, in the course of his daily Press briefing, and said, "We 
recognise the validity of the unanimous decision of the United Nations 
Security Council, Resolution 1441, under  Chapter VII of the UN Charter. 
We note that Iraq has accepted the term s of the Resolution, and that the UN 
Inspectors have commenced their work. Iraq has had to faithfully comply 
with the provisions of this Resolution. We have consistently stated that if 
Iraq complies fully with the provisions of the Security Council Resolution, 
sanctions against that country should be lifted. If Iraq does not comply with 
UN Security Council Resolution 1441, the Security Council should decide on 
what action should be taken. We sincerely hope in the interests of humanity, 
that this matter can be resolved peacefully through the United Nations". This 
Statement, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, wa s issued very recently - I think, on 
November 21 or 22. 
In the meanwhile, there was an occasio n, because as many Members have 
referred to non-alignment, when we were in New York for the Non-aligned 
Foreign Ministers' meet, on the sidelin es of the UNGA took place. I also 
participated, on behalf of India, in that meeting. The Non-Aligned Movement 
adopted a Resolution on Iraq, and subsequently, at the initiative of the Non-
Aligned Movement, led by its current Chairman, namely, South Africa, it 
was decided in the U.N. that the U.N.  Security Council shall have an open 
debate in which all members coul d participate an d the Permanent 
Representative of India participated in that debate which was held on 
October 17, 2002. This was before U.N. Security Council Resolution 1441 
was debated. What did the Permanent Representative of India say? I think, 
this is the most comprehensive and authoritative exposition of India's point 
of view at no other forum but the Security Council of the United Nations. I 
am quoting some extracts from it. He said, "In contemplating use of force, 
the question of legitimacy and the international rule of law are important. 
India recognises the desire of the international community to see the full 
compliance by Iraq of all relevant U.N.  Resolutions, including those relating 
to the repatriation of Kuwaiti and third country nationals and return of all 
Kuwaiti property. Such a desire, however, cannot justify any unilateral action 
on Iraq without the agreement of the U.N." He went on to say, "We are of the 
view that given the current configur ation of circumstances, any undermining 
of the territorial integrity of Iraq could have unforeseen and 
271 

RAJYA SABHA [28 November. 2002] 
destructive geo-political implications. This could extend even beyond the 
region." Then, at another point, with regard to the discussion of U.N. 
Security Council Resolution which was going on, he said, "We believe that 
the conditions attached to any new Resolution or the modalities of their 
implementation should not be such as to make them unworkable or 
effectively to invite their rejection." Then, he talked about sanctions and he 
talked about how use of force should be  avoided. This was the statement of 
the Indian representative to the U.N. Security Council of which incidentally 
we are not a member, at this point of time, but because NAM took the 
initiative, all got a chance to say what they felt, and we made this statement. 
So, both in our public and in our private conversations - public 
statements and private conversations - what is the point of view India has 
always held? One, no unilateralism, but  only U.N. action. Two, Iraq should 
comply with the U.N. Resolutions. Th ree, sanctions should be'lifted in 
tandem with full and effective compliance of this, and avoidance of military 
conflict, avoidance of war and seek ing solution through peaceful means. 
This has been the position of India which has been repeatedly given 
expression to.

sent a Special Envoy. Thei r Minister for Informati on came to India, as the 
special envoy of President Saddam Hussein: He had a meeting with his 
counterpart, the Information and- Broadcasting Minister of India; he had a

Three, and very important, he expressed his fullest satisfaction with the
